I did not answer him at the time because the question was wrong, so here is the answer now. He asked whether that era defined us. It did not. It shaped us, which is a different verb, and the difference matters more than it sounds. I used to think nostalgia was harmless. I do not any more. It is not that the memories are false. It is that memory keeps the Sunday and quietly throws away the Tuesday, and then you compare a life made of Tuesdays to a highlight reel and you lose, every time. Those were the days is a sentence about a phase. When somebody says it about a whole life, listen carefully, because they are usually telling you something about right now.

For two hundred years nostalgia was classified as an illness. Doctors wrote it up as a disorder of soldiers far from home, and they proposed treatments for it, some of them unpleasant. The modern research says almost the opposite. When people are asked to remember a period they loved, they come out of it measurably more optimistic, more generous and more willing to try something new. That is a strange result for an illness. The current explanation is that nostalgia is not about the past at all. It is a way of reminding yourself that you have been someone before, which is the evidence you need to believe you can be someone again. The people it damages are the ones who use it as a place to live rather than a place to visit.
